title: Code Quest Parents' Catch Up
note: Lightly cleaned. Speaker names corrected, crosstalk and false starts removed. The full automatic transcript is in the linked doc.

turns.w: They really enjoyed it. I could see that Ezekiel enjoyed it and everybody enjoyed it as well. So one, I think it's good to keep it going. I was talking to BJ about it. There's probably other things that can be done, so I was just asking what's the next step and how do we get it going, because I thought it's a really good project.

Thanks Gbenga. I will try my best to keep this fairly short, because the point of this for me is I really want to hear from you all as opposed to me talking at you a lot. But I did want to use this opportunity to share where Code Quest has got to, share a couple of thoughts as to where it could go, and ask you a couple of questions.

Thanks for making the time. I know each of us has a lot going on. And actually a special thanks to Ayo and Lina, because it's your anniversary weekend. I know giving up your time, and your weekend, I'm sure you could be doing other things. So the fact that you took the time, it means a lot. Happy anniversary to you both again.
We know God has been faithful to you. And our prayer, my prayer, is that he keeps blessing your marriage, your home, and your family for many, many more years.

I'm really excited about where Code Quest is. From conversations I've had and things I've heard and seen, I think we're all excited. It's been really great and rewarding to see how it's all unfolded. The kids have worked together. They've built amazing things.

What has struck me the most was how seriously they all took it. They all worked hard. They had a real drive to see it through. I remember the night before, none of them slept properly. They were all doing pre-work on their projects. Nobody asked them to do that. It's a good show of how interested and excited they were. There was a bit of a fire that was lit.
I was just laughing at the photo of Theodore and his drink. But it looks very professional. It looks like one of these startup kind of things. It's really good.
Yeah. Silicon Valley.
They really tried, and to be fair a lot of it was self-managed. They worked amongst themselves. It was only a bit of light facilitation on our part.

It's been good for the kids and it's also been good for us. Watching them work together has been the best part of it. But actually the things they produced, if I'm being honest, it's not just kid standard. It's top standard, as somebody that works in the AI space. They hit really good standards of excellence in what they built collectively. And for us as parents, it was a moment of pride.

I was talking to Arthur yesterday, asking what was the best part of the holiday they enjoyed, and they really enjoy just being with all the cousins. Out of all the different things, that's the thing they enjoy the most. And Code Quest is a big chunk of that.

Let's take a look at some of the things they created. This is something Ezekiel and his team created. Serious stuff. This is the music video the Pixel Power team created, AI generated videos. Math Kingdom that Sophia and her team created. This one would be the one Emma created. Emma is actually vibe coding now. And of course Theodore's one, the Dragonball. These are all working apps.

An interesting thing. I've been having conversations with a couple of us, and one of them was with Grandma, where I was trying to explain that actually this whole thing is not about AI. It has AI on the front but it's actually not about AI.

The kids were awarded prizes that had nothing to do with AI. Sophia got best presenter, Ezekiel got best team leader, Elsie got most creative, Hannah got overcomer, Theodore was calm under pressure, Arthur had perseverance, Emma was participation. These are all examples of the non-technical skills that are required for general development as leaders and people that would go on to succeed.

So if we were to ask the question, what actually is Code Quest? There are about five pillars, or a flywheel. You play something. They consumed the games we were making together. They made their own. They can put it out there. People can see it. They can share it. And then they can make more.

It's not just about coding. Coding is just the medium. It's really about an identity of being somebody who is a builder, somebody who is a creator. And through that there are other skill sets they develop, and we've seen elements of it in the first couple of Code Quests. They can be a maker, a publisher, a mentor, and ultimately an owner.
Thanks to Aunty Mai for her input on product thinking and product direction, in terms of how Code Quest could be repositioned to not just coding.
I made a game. Mum said it was all right to put it up. Now it lives on the internet at its own address. Anyone can go there. I'm nine. I built that.

There's momentum. One of the pieces of feedback I was getting from speaking to the kids and a couple of us is there's momentum, and this could be a moment where, if we're willing, we could come together on it and take it to whatever the next steps are.

There are two things I would love to explore with all of us. One is the next Code Quest with our kids. When can we do that, and what does it look like. And separately, something I would love to invite our thinking on is whether this could go beyond our family.

So Code Quest 3. How soon could we do it, and what does it look like? Given the journey the kids have been on and what they've produced, I've got some ideas on what that looks like, but I would also love to open it up so we can think about it together, and try to keep pace around it.

My second ask is beyond our family. How could this be extended or offered or shared outside the four walls? I have some ideas, but granted I have had a lot of time to think about it, and I would rather we thought about it together.

One is potentially a rebrand, because as it's evolved it's really not about code only. Then there's this concept of co-delivery. Around the table, we're very rich in experience and years of service in various things, that have afforded us a lot of skill that would be of much value, and not just in the area of code or tech.

Co-delivery means could we work on delivering things in person together, but also co-delivery on an app, where things could be shared by way of instructions, training, learnings, things that would help the Code Quest kids.

Other ideas are physical events. Imagine if we did Code Quest in other locations, a similar structure, but we extend it to other kids and work with their parents. There's a concept of a learning journey, a developmental ladder necessary to achieve the milestones of being a builder, a creator, and putting things into the world. Presentation skills, leadership skills, emotional intelligence, product skills, tech. Amongst us, and I mean all of us including Grandma, we all have skills that would be massively valuable.

Here's a very quick visualisation of what an app could look like. It's not in any way final, it's just a concept. The kids could log on. Parents can log in and authorise things, approve things or not approve things depending on how they see fit. Parents can see the kids' activity, control what they're looking at, what they're sharing, and how much time they spend on the app.

The kids can see the schedule for the next event, share videos and content, see where they're at on their journey, and make stuff using the app. It's purely a mockup. It could look completely different and might not even have any of these functions.

These are just my ideas. Nothing is final. What I'd really love is to hear what everyone else is thinking. Ultimately the real question for me is, could this be something that we do together, in whatever capacity that looks like? And whatever this becomes, the part that is most important to me is, can we do this together as a family?

We've got our scripture, Psalm 16 verse 6. The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places, and yes, I have a goodly heritage. And one can chase a thousand, two can put ten thousand to flight. So this is really us being a unit, a mastermind. There's so much we could achieve together.

I think all the things you're saying, absolutely. Can we do another Code Quest? Absolutely. They would love to do it. I really like the idea that it's not just the coding thing. How can we equip them with skills they can use wherever they are? I think that's wonderful.
It's possible this could be a global thing. I'm sure there are other families who would love the opportunity to put their kids through this, for the end product of who they become on the other side.

The kids became a bit of a sore point. I was like, I don't want to hear the words Code Quest for the next day please. But yeah, really good. I thought the app is really good as well. A nice touch would be, when kids come on, depending on their age range, maybe our kids could be the pillars. If you're between five and seven, Emma is your bot. She talks with her voice, and that guides you through. So the kids are the face of it, based on their age range.
I like that. I do like the idea of the kids being a face, or being mentors, because it's good to find a way to get them engaged. Invested, as well.

One thing I was thinking. You had a page that said, what should we do now, should we do this, should we do that. I'd almost say order the things that we could do next, to answer what's the next question.

Right now the thesis around it's more than coding doesn't necessarily mean you need to do the branding now. It's really just between us. What would the value of that be at this point? Rather than working backwards from, it looks great and has the right name, what's the next action we want, or the next outcome we want from it? Is it that we want to prove that people outside of our children are interested in it? Then that becomes the next thing.

Almost have a milestone plan that says at this point it makes sense to rebrand, because we would have proved certain things with these outcomes. A chart that has the outcomes we're trying to prove at each stage. It gives us the data point we need to decide what we do next.

For example, would it make sense to do a physical interaction. Is that like a hosting party? Could we do a hosting party in Chappaqua? We wanted to do a hackathon with the kids in the basement, and this is a really good template shell to run a hackathon at home instead, and it's more structured. Could that be the next thing we want to prove, that people outside of our children actually want to do this? I think that's more important than doing a branding exercise.

I love the idea Lina had with the kids being the voices, because especially as you said, Emma. I thought it's nice for a five year old to hear another five year old talking. It would be really engaging.

When you showed the pictures of the kids doing Code Quest, it reminded me again of how engaged they really were. I remember Sophia was really articulate when she was talking about, I don't use enough tech, so I'm really looking forward to getting stuck in and exploring tech more. And she really transformed when she was on that stage to present their project.

So what would be really good for the next Code Quest is if they work on individual projects, and they all work on it by themselves, and then they get a chance to present what they have worked on on their own. It was great for them to work as a team, because it's nice to have that challenge to see how you work together in a trio, but it would also be quite nice to see them individually.

And for us not to just judge them on the AI, but on the other things as well. On their soft skills, on their presentation skills, on the cadence of their voice and what they show us on the screen. So almost have the AI at the bottom of the thing that we're ranking, but give them an opportunity to work on these other things that we're saying are really important for them to develop.
Doing it in person gives a different vibe than an online thing, and I feel like it's more impactful when they can do that. To start it is a good way, and then to anchor it back every once in a while.

The other thing, and this is where maybe the app comes into play more, is giving them autonomy to go and practise it by themselves in their own environment. Once they are in the together environment, it's done for them. But if you can then say, here is something you can go and practise by yourself, that is easy for them to execute and to share. That's where the app will come in very useful. You were able to do it before, and now you can go and do it at home, where it's harder to set up by yourself.

And it's about the output, not the tools to get it. That's why I said the AI or the coding bit should be facilitator, not the meat of the thing. It makes us able to deliver it better, and maybe they can use it, but it's a tool, not necessarily the special sauce.

The other thing that's interesting is the monetisation of it eventually. Having this skill or this thing that you build is good, but how do you make it more than that? How do you turn it into a business? What are the things inside it? How do you get other people to do it? That's another dimension that could be added. That's a next stage of something interesting.

I don't understand it enough to be able to make comments, because I find all the jargon that you guys are using interesting, and I follow. But one thing I want to say is, I don't know what this is leading to. Maybe you get to the point where you involve other people, or you sell it to other people. Not selling by money, but get people interested.

The point I'm trying to make is that you have to take on board every child's temperament. As you're doing these things, with much of their creativity and all the things they are putting in, you have to take into consideration their temperament.

The last one that we did, we talked about their presentation skills, because that's what I know, presentation skills and the visual image you get from what they presented. But we have to take into consideration their different temperaments and how to make comments and how to deal with them within those temperaments. It's very important to take into consideration their temperament as you try to praise them, as you try to encourage them. I don't think we need to push them. They already have the thing to go for it. But I think we should take into consideration each child's temperament.

I do think each person gets something different from it. Ezekiel is very driven, he can just sit there and work. Arthur benefits from the fact that everybody was there, and then he gets motivated by osmosis. I like the fact that there's now a cohort of people that allows them to be reasonably accountable.

I think you could do it two different ways. One is specifically for our children, how can you use it to cultivate different life lessons. And then how do you take all the things you learn from that and use it in a more scalable way.

For me, what I want in particular is, can you do something every single day at a particular time and work towards something. What's your goal? Okay, every day you have to do this, and that's your goal. And if you're doing this on an app, that's something the whole group can see. Ayo can say, Arthur, you've not done this today, I looked at your streaks. It takes a village to raise a child. That allows the cohort to not just be the parents saying this is your goal.

Essentially this is a learning path. Just like school, school has to deal with different people at different times, and there are the skills of the people who are the facilitators. You have to recognise the differences and connect the people who are involved.

All of these things are about knowledge, but we're supposed to be open about the place we're trying to get them to. We would have ideas for our own children, but even if we were just to use those things, I think other people we may want to subscribe to whatever protocol would also be interested. I want my child to go through the process because I need them to go in this area. I think both things can be achieved by this.
That's interesting, because I didn't think of it as a learning platform. But essentially it does become that. It is helping them to learn many different things.

That was why there was a bit of wrestling with the name of Code Quest. You come to it for one thing, what it says on the tin, but you leave with so much more. Let's say somebody goes to a martial arts lesson. You're not going there to learn how to fight. You're going to achieve your black belt, but you're also going to learn how to regulate yourself emotionally, how to handle conflict, how to centre yourself. There's the shop window, what you get, and then there's a whole bunch of other stuff at the end.

My recommendation for right now is, what is the next step? There are two offshoots. There's the next Code Quest for our kids, and then there's this exploratory journey of whether we can prove that other kids outside the Olatoye family could do it. Maybe we put two stakes in the ground. One as to when's the date of the next Code Quest for the family, and one for how we're going to test the idea outside the family.

Can I add to that the constraint of, what is the question we answer by doing the next one? I ask that not because we just want to do it for our kids, but because we want to make this a business. What is the data or feedback we want back from doing the next one?
I understand the question, and I agree with your line of thinking, but where my head is at is the kids have started a journey. How do we just keep it going?

You're answering my question. Actually I disagree, I don't think you keep them separate. What you're saying is the stage we're at is we're trying to design the programme, trying to create the harness around what this thing is actually going to be that makes it valuable for our kids first, and then we can offer it to other people. I don't think that's fully mapped out yet. A lot of ideas have been said today.
I could see it for Ezekiel. I think Ezekiel would be very interested to see how he gets his app somewhere that somebody else can play with it.
I can see it for Elsie too. Elsie is already creating content, almost following the pathway intuitively. I've just released this game, here is the link.
I've just made the craziest games on my website and they are recently added. You can play them with the link that I put in the description.

What I meant was, could people see what the kids want to get out of it? Theodore I think soon would want to push it out there somewhere. What do you think they see as the next stage that will make them excited? It's keeping that excitement rolling that I'm thinking about.

Definitely interested in getting this game out there. He's interested in how can I get the game out there. I do think both of them would be excited to make it become something they can do. All of them, even the girls, would be interested in the ability to have the things they produce on the app for everybody to see.

Can I make an observation from somebody who is not very knowledgeable about AI. When they've been together, bonding as cousins, they were all very relaxed, nothing was serious, they jumped here and jumped there. But when it came to doing their presentations, everybody was serious. It was like a project. I was almost afraid. There was nobody poking anybody, nobody doing anything. Everybody was waiting for what they were going to do.

Another question I want to ask. If you went somewhere and you got a bunch of people who are technologically aware like you guys are, and you said Code Quest, is there anything like that? Will it mean the same thing that we're doing here?

There is a terminology called a hackathon. Arthur described it well. The first Code Quest, it's a coding party. But what it really means is a hands-on workshop where you start off the day with the desire to build something, and you end the day with that thing built, and the journey from the start to the end is facilitated. It's almost identical to what we did at Native. A briefing session beforehand, a briefing in the morning, blocks of work, lunch, snacks, prep for presentation, presentation, judging. It's not a concept that would be unfamiliar for someone to grasp.

One of the challenges we faced even at the Code Quest event was that nobody knows off the top of their head how to get their app on the app store. What we wanted to do with Code Quest is remove the need for that question at all. If we put the Code Quest app on the app store, and this concept of the marketplace, then Ezekiel can say, I've got this ninja app, I'm going to share it with you on WhatsApp. That takes them to download Code Quest and get his app, but it also onboards them onto Code Quest. Then it's, all these other people are on Code Quest, I would love to learn what Ezekiel did, so let me join the next cohort.
Basically you control the system, isn't it. To get the app you come to us. To put your app, you come to us.

Eventually you could even say you can build on the app. Ezekiel sends the ninja game to somebody else, and then everybody can start using that to do more things, and it makes it easier for somebody who doesn't have all the setup easily available to come on board. It's hard when you're not physically with somebody that can help you.

The app can be monetised from advertisements, in-app advertisements, which the Code Quest team, us, can manage. As far as the builder, the kid, is concerned, all they need to do is push their stuff on Code Quest and share it. The people playing will see ads, and that ad revenue will come to the Code Quest platform, and then a portion of it will be sent to the kids.

Having something that involves kids means you have to be careful about visibility. It'll be interesting to see how you can respect parents' wishes inside it. One parent might say you can't show your face, one parent might say don't put their name. You can still get a lot out of it, and talk to different people, based on what the parents allow.

I think you can do the next one with our kids, because by the sounds of it there's still more work to do. Your point about, is Ezekiel further ahead, is this person, there's still that question to answer. So I don't think we need to do an external party with other people just yet.
How do you want to tackle it? The Olatoye kids are driven, so they are hard on themselves when they evaluate themselves. How do you want to deal with that?
It's a really good question. There's nothing wrong with being hard on yourself. You might find a good way to reverse engineer that, using the mentorship idea as part of it.

From my point of view, part of the soft skills, one of the skills they may learn, is the giving and receiving of feedback. Understanding how to take that feedback, and how you deal with people saying no, that wasn't good, or no, you didn't win, and that's okay.
With our children we practise saying no on purpose. Not because we don't want to say yes, but so that you can hear no and understand that you will survive.
That was a big one this time, because there were some people who thought they had done really well.

This is why I think it's useful to understand it as a learning platform, because for me it's almost akin to parenting. What do I want them to be able to deal with in five years' time, ten years' time? One of those things is, I am not going to be in every room that you are in. So you're going to have to deal with people who may not be for you, or people who don't necessarily see everything that you bring to the table.

As a family we're doing everything we can to fortify them and help them grow and support them. However, the ability to hear feedback that might not be pleasant is a skill. Sometimes it might sound better coming from Uncle Ayo saying, listen, I think you could maybe do this here, or Uncle B saying it. It helps them, because sometimes they can drown us out, but it's good for them because we all share the same values.

This is a safe space. A no from me, however harsh that might feel, is still going to be less harsh than a no from somebody who's not invested in you. And there are probably going to be conversations to say, can we document what our shared values are, and what it is that we want to leave them with, in character and personality. Because all of us are different. However, there are things that we have all had to learn to operate in a professional environment that are universal.

They actually experienced that in Code Quest. Some of the Code Questers were very sure they had knocked it out of the park and did really good work, but the feedback we gave them was very objective, and some of it was not what they were expecting to hear. It was a visible blow. I could see they took that a little bit hard. But what we also stressed in the room was, this is the room where it will be the safest place, hopefully ever. This is the place where we want you to hear this kind of feedback.

There's also a converse. The ability to articulate your thoughts. Think about Dragons' Den. There's the dragon, who is the authority, and the person you should have deference to and respect, all of that is correct. But there are sometimes when the pitcher has to stand up to the dragon, not disrespectfully, but you've got to have the fortitude to be assertive. That is an emotion that needs training. If there's a real argument you can articulate confidently, that should also be trained and encouraged, because we want these people to go out into the world and challenge. These are lawyers, these are public speakers.

We're over time, so I just want to make sure, what are the concrete steps? One, pick a time for the next one. And it may be interesting for each person to go in and just describe how they see it evolving into the next steps. Maybe voice notes or whatever. And then let's pull all those things together to see how that evolves, because everybody has a different one, and there's no way that all the ideas can work. But record them anyway. It might be, this is stage one, this is stage two, this is stage three.

I disagree with Mai when she said don't put the brand name. I think it's interesting to say, what is this thing? But if the next stage is just with the kids, what's the point in spending the effort yet? I guess work in parallel.

So go away in the next few days and just record it. This is what I think about it, and drop it somewhere, and then we use that to figure out all the different things that people said, and develop that in parallel. What are you building here for the kids, and how could that translate into something we can take outside?

I agree, I think it's a great idea. Just to help with admin, WhatsApp is going to be a tricky place, because conversations will get lost. Let me send you guys a link where we can just organise our thoughts, and you can drop your voice notes or written notes, because then it will be logged and organised. It will take a little bit of effort to do that, but it will save a lot of time on the back end.
If we're waiting for weekends, the 22nd we are out and about. Friday the 21st works for us. Thursday the 20th works, or Thursday the 27th. So for us the earliest we can do is the 29th.
For me I can probably only do weekends.

Can I ask a question. When we say the next Code Quest, what are we talking about? Are we talking about the day the kids present, or the day we're giving the kids the assignment? Because for us, we can't do this coming weekend, we can't do next weekend. They're probably not available until mid to end of September if it's a weekend. So that's why I'm asking, what are we doing, so that we know.

If it's three hours, if we can make it much smaller chunks. Let's say we introduce them to something they can start doing themselves, we do it on one day and say, you get this and you start doing it yourselves. Then that specific one doesn't need to be that long.

This is why I was asking what we're doing in the next one. If it's just, we need an hour, all the kids are on it, we give them the instructions, and then we meet again three weeks later, then we know what time we need to carve out.

I think we need a pathway, which might look like a bit of a syllabus. One thing I don't think we can do is replicate what we just did at Code Quest number two in a week, because that was quite heavy. But we've already established that Code Quest can be multiple things. It could be a session on speaking. It could be a session on emotional intelligence.

And we may not necessarily need all of us to be there. If we're doing this together, maybe the next session might be one of you doing a session on the non-technical, EQ side of things that contribute to the bigger picture.
Every week is too much. At least for me.

It might be interesting to say, here is a syllabus, on this day you have to do this. That makes it easier for it to be executed, and it's less strain on every individual person. We just say, here's the syllabus, do the thing. And in the meantime, if we can get the app to a place where they can also be doing something by themselves as well. Those two things in parallel, I think that'll be a good way to move it forward. And let's try to make it an hour or so, or 45 minutes.
If we're doing a session, I would recommend that it's always recorded, just so we have it for the log and we can put it into whatever platform we need later. That would be my one ask.

And the second ask, if we're doing this periodic schedule, should we put a stake in the ground for a larger milestone? Week one we're doing this training, week two we're doing that thing, but it would be nice for them to work towards something that is the summit of what they've worked towards. The next big presentation, where we all aim to be there as the judges. And prior to that, the milestones in between, maybe we can divvy up to whoever's available.

I agree. And I'm not trying to shy away from a session at all, but because they have previously experienced Code Quest as an opportunity to come and create the game, I feel like the next Code Quest should still be that. And in that session we introduce, guys listen, we're expanding this. Different weeks, people are going to come and teach you different things.

Maybe you're going to come up with a way of how you can take the lesson you've learned and technise it and use the AI skills. On the days we're talking about emotional resilience, the challenge could be how can you use this. Because quite frankly, the thing that excites them the most is the tech side, the creative side. So we want to make sure we don't lose that, but we want to feed in the lessons that they don't even know they're learning through it. You've delivered this session on how to speak, these were the key five points, now make a presentation so that a child your age can engage with this.
Let's pick a date which is what, two weeks away, and let's develop what that thing is going to be and what the syllabus is going to be. Two weeks away gives us some time. Is that your 29th?
That's good.
If we do it for 45 minutes at an appropriate time, is that workable?
It depends what we end up doing for our anniversary that weekend. But we should be able to fit it in. Let us come back to you on that.

Let's develop it on chat. 29th tentatively. I'm conscious of time, I don't want to keep everybody too long. So we picked a rough date, but maybe we adjust it over WhatsApp. And if we can figure out that link for how to chat about the next thing, that'd be very useful. Thanks a lot. Thanks everybody.
